e-7118.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
e-7118.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in\left[0,1\right].$
e-7118.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

e-9517.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
e-9517.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^3\,\mathrm{d}x + z\,\mathrm{d}y + y\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $\mathbf{r}(t)=2t\,\mathbf{i} + \cos t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in[0,\pi]?$
e-9517.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

e-9528.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C y\,\mathrm{d}x -x\,\mathrm{d}y ,$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in[0,\pi].$
e-9528.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = \cos t, \qquad
y(t) = 3\sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =-3{t|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: With x=1/t and y=t, we have dx/dt=-1/t² and dy/dt=1. Thus xy²(dx/dt)+(1/x)(dy/dt)=-1/t+t=(t²-1)/t, giving option e.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxy2dx+1xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=1ti+tj for t∈[1,3]?

a
∫13t−1tdt
b
∫132tdt
c
∫13t2+1tdt
d
2∫131tdt
e
∫13t2−1tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=1t,y(t)=t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(1t)i+ddt(t)j=−1t2i+j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxy2dx+1xdy=∫13xy2dxdtdt+1xdydtdt=∫13(xy2dxdt+1xdydt)dt=∫131t⋅t2⋅(−1t2)+1(1t)⋅1dt=∫13−1t+tdt=∫13t2−1tdt

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=(t−2)i+(t3−t)j for t∈[1,2]?

a
∫12t(4t2−1)dt
b
∫124t3−3t−2dt
c
∫124t3+t−2dt
d
∫124t3−t−2dt
e
∫124t3−2dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Here x=t-2, y=t³-t, x'=1, and y'=3t²-1. The integrand becomes (x+y)x'+(x+2)y'=(t³-2)+t(3t²-1)=4t³-t-2. Therefore option d is equivalent.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t-2)\,i+({t}^{3}-t)\,j$ for $t\in [1,2]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j \\  & =i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=(t−2)i+(t3−t)j for t∈[1,2]?

a
∫12t(4t2−1)dt
b
∫124t3−3t−2dt
c
∫124t3+t−2dt
d
∫124t3−t−2dt
e
∫124t3−2dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t−2,y(t)=t3−t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(t−2)i+ddt(t3−t)j=i+(3t2−1)j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy=∫12(x+y)dxdtdt+(x+2)dydtdt=∫12((x+y)dxdt+(x+2)dydt)dt=∫12(t−2+t3−t)⋅1+(t−2+2)⋅(3t2−1)dt=∫12t3−2+3t3−tdt=∫124t3−t−2dt

verification.explanation: Substituting x=t-2, y=t³-t, dx=dt, and dy=(3t²-1)dt gives (t³-2)+t(3t²-1)=4t³-t-2. This confirms option d and agrees with the revealed worked solution; the displayed incorrect submission selected b.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t-2)\,i+({t}^{3}-t)\,j$ for $t\in [1,2]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j \\  & =i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−2y)dx+xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=(t+1)i−2t2j for t∈[−1,1]?

a
∫−111−3tdt
b
∫−111−4tdt
c
∫−118t2+4t+1dt
d
∫−111−3t−8t2dt
e
∫−111−5tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: With x=t+1, y=-2t², x'=1, and y'=-4t, the integrand is (t+1+4t²)-4t(t+1)=1-3t, giving a directly. Options b and e also have the same integral value, 2, because their odd terms integrate to zero on [-1,1].

after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t+1)\,i-2{t}^{2}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t+1,\,y(t)=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+(-4t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(x-2y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}((x-2y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(t+1-2\cdot (-2{t}^{2}))\cdot 1+(t+1)\cdot (-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t+1+4{t}^{2}-4{t}^{2}-4t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}1-3t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−2y)dx+xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=(t+1)i−2t2j for t∈[−1,1]?

a
∫−111−3tdt
b
∫−111−4tdt
c
∫−118t2+4t+1dt
d
∫−111−3t−8t2dt
e
∫−111−5tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t+1,y(t)=−2t2.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(t+1)i+ddt(−2t2)j=i+(−4t)j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C(x−2y)dx+xdy=∫−11(x−2y)dxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫−11((x−2y)dxdt+xdydt)dt=∫−11(t+1−2⋅(−2t2))⋅1+(t+1)⋅(−4t)dt=∫−11t+1+4t2−4t2−4tdt=∫−111−3tdt

$$

$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$

before.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dx+(y−x)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=2sin⁡ti−2cos⁡tj for t∈[0,π2]?

a
2∫0π/2dt
b
4∫0π/2dt
c
2∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
d
4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/22cos⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Here x=2sin(t), y=-2cos(t), x'=2cos(t), and y'=2sin(t). Thus (x-y)x'+(y-x)y'=4(sin(t)+cos(t))(cos(t)-sin(t))=4cos(2t), giving option d directly. Option c also has the same integral value, zero.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}((x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dx+(y−x)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=2sin⁡ti−2cos⁡tj for t∈[0,π2]?

a
2∫0π/2dt
b
4∫0π/2dt
c
2∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
d
4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/22cos⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=2sin⁡t,y(t)=−2cos⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2sin⁡t)i+ddt(−2cos⁡t)j=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C(x−y)dx+(y−x)dy=∫0π/2(x−y)dxdtdt+(y−x)dydtdt=∫0π/2((x−y)dxdt+(y−x)dydt)dt=∫0π/2(2sin⁡t−(−2cos⁡t))⋅2cos⁡t+(−2cos⁡t−2sin⁡t)⋅2sin⁡tdt=∫0π/24sin⁡tcos⁡t+4cos2⁡t−4cos⁡tsin⁡t−4sin2⁡tdt=∫0π/24(cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t)dt=∫0π/24cos⁡(2t)dt=4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt

verification.explanation: Substitution gives (x-y)x'+(y-x)y'=4(cos²(t)-sin²(t))=4cos(2t), confirming option d and the revealed solution. Option c has the same value, zero, but d is the direct parametrization. The displayed incorrect submission selected b.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}((x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydx+xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=eti+et+1j for t∈[0,1]?

a
2∫01e2t+1dt
b
∫01e3t+1+e2t+1dt
c
2∫01e3t+1dt
d
∫01e5t+2dt
e
∫01e3t+e2tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: With x=e^t and y=e^(t+1), we have x'=e^t and y'=e^(t+1). Therefore xyx'+xy'=e^(3t+1)+e^(2t+1), giving option b.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{t},\,y(t)={e}^{t+1}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t+1})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{3t+1}+{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydx+xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=eti+et+1j for t∈[0,1]?

a
2∫01e2t+1dt
b
∫01e3t+1+e2t+1dt
c
2∫01e3t+1dt
d
∫01e5t+2dt
e
∫01e3t+e2tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=et,y(t)=et+1.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(et)i+ddt(et+1)j=eti+et+1j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxydx+xdy=∫01xydxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫01(xydxdt+xdydt)dt=∫01et⋅et+1⋅et+et⋅et+1dt=∫01e3t+1+e2t+1dt

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{t},\,y(t)={e}^{t+1}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t+1})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{3t+1}+{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C2ydx+ln⁡xdy+3zdz, where C is a portion of the curve r(t)=i+tj+t2k for t∈[1,3]?

a
∫135ln⁡t+2dt
b
∫136t2dt
c
∫13t2+5ln⁡tdt
d
∫133t2+2dt
e
∫13t3−2ln⁡tdt

decision.explanation: The parametrization gives x=1, y=t, z=t², so x'=0, y'=1, and z'=2t. Hence the integrand is 2t·0+ln(1)·1+3t²·2t=6t³. The equivalent integral is ∫₁³6t³ dt=120. None of the displayed options equals this integral.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2y\,dx+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,dy+3z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=\,i+t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=1,\,y(t)=t,\,z(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2y\,dx+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,dy+3z\,dz & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+3z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2t\cdot (0)+\operatorname{ln}⁡1\cdot (1)+3{t}^{2}\cdot (2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}6{t}^{2}\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C2ydx+ln⁡xdy+3zdz, where C is a portion of the curve r(t)=i+tj+t2k for t∈[1,3]?

a
∫135ln⁡t+2dt
b
∫136t2dt
c
∫13t2+5ln⁡tdt
d
∫133t2+2dt
e
∫13t3−2ln⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=1,y(t)=t,z(t)=t2.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(1)i+ddt(t)j+ddt(t2)k=j+2tk.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C2ydx+ln⁡xdy+3zdz=∫132ydxdtdt+ln⁡xdydtdt+3zdzdtdt=∫13(2ydxdt+ln⁡xdydt+3zdzdt)dt=∫132t⋅(0)+ln⁡1⋅(1)+3t2⋅(2t)dt=∫136t2dt

before.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx3dx+zdy+ydz, where C is a portion of the helix r(t)=ti+cos⁡tj+sin⁡tk for t∈[0,π]?

a
∫0πcos⁡2t+sin⁡tdt
b
∫0πt3+cos⁡2tdt
c
∫0πcos3⁡tdt
d
∫0πt2−cos⁡tdt
e
∫0πcos2⁡t+1dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Here x=t, y=cos(t), z=sin(t), with derivatives 1, -sin(t), and cos(t). Thus x³x'+zy'+yz'=t³-sin²(t)+cos²(t)=t³+cos(2t), giving option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\pi ]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}\cdot (1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx3dx+zdy+ydz, where C is a portion of the helix r(t)=ti+cos⁡tj+sin⁡tk for t∈[0,π]?

a
∫0πcos⁡2t+sin⁡tdt
b
∫0πt3+cos⁡2tdt
c
∫0πcos3⁡tdt
d
∫0πt2−cos⁡tdt
e
∫0πcos2⁡t+1dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t,y(t)=cos⁡t,z(t)=sin⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(t)i+ddt(cos⁡t)j+ddt(sin⁡t)k=i−sin⁡tj+cos⁡tk.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cx3dx+zdy+ydz=∫0πx3dxdtdt+zdydtdt+ydzdtdt=∫0π(x3dxdt+zdydt+ydzdt)dt=∫0πt3⋅(1)+sin⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+cos⁡t⋅(cos⁡t)dt=∫0πt3+cos2⁡t−sin2⁡tdt=∫0πt3+cos⁡2tdt

verification.explanation: Substituting x=t, y=cos(t), z=sin(t) and their derivatives gives t³−sin²(t)+cos²(t)=t³+cos(2t). This confirms option b and agrees with the revealed solution. The incorrect submission selected d.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\pi ]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}\cdot (1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C−ydx+xdy+zdz, where C is a portion of the helix r(t)=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj+tk for t∈[π4,π3]?

a
∫π/4π/3t2+9dt
b
∫π/4π/3t2+cos2⁡tdt
c
∫π/4π/3t2−sin⁡tdt
d
∫π/4π/3t+2cos⁡2tdt
e
∫π/4π/3t+2dt
Submit

decision.explanation: With x=√2 cos(t), y=√2 sin(t), and z=t, the integrand becomes -yx'+xy'+zz'=2sin²(t)+2cos²(t)+t=t+2. Therefore option e is equivalent.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{3}]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C−ydx+xdy+zdz, where C is a portion of the helix r(t)=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj+tk for t∈[π4,π3]?

a
∫π/4π/3t2+9dt
b
∫π/4π/3t2+cos2⁡tdt
c
∫π/4π/3t2−sin⁡tdt
d
∫π/4π/3t+2cos⁡2tdt
e
∫π/4π/3t+2dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=2cos⁡t,y(t)=2sin⁡t,z(t)=t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j+ddt(t)k=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj+k.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C−ydx+xdy+zdz=∫π/4π/3−ydxdtdt+xdydtdt+zdzdtdt=∫π/4π/3(−ydxdt+xdydt+zdzdt)dt=∫π/4π/3−2sin⁡t⋅(−2sin⁡t)+2cos⁡t⋅(2cos⁡t)+t⋅1dt=∫π/4π/3t+2sin2⁡t+2cos2⁡tdt=∫π/4π/3t+2dt

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{3}]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Czdx+ydy−xdz, where C is a portion of the curve r(t)=3cos⁡ti+t2j+3sin⁡tk for t∈[0,π2]?

a
∫0π/22t2+3cos2⁡tdt
b
∫0π/2t4−2dt
c
∫0π/22t3−9dt
d
∫0π/22t2+3sin2⁡tdt
e
∫0π/2t−sin2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: With x=3cos(t), y=t², z=3sin(t), their derivatives are -3sin(t), 2t, and 3cos(t). Thus zx'+yy'-xz'=-9sin²(t)+2t³-9cos²(t)=2t³-9, giving option c.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}z\,dx+y\,dy-x\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)={t}^{2},\,z(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}z\,dx+y\,dy-x\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}z\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(z\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{t}^{2}\cdot (2t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{t}^{3}-9{sin}^{2}⁡t-9{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{t}^{3}-9\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Czdx+ydy−xdz, where C is a portion of the curve r(t)=3cos⁡ti+t2j+3sin⁡tk for t∈[0,π2]?

a
∫0π/22t2+3cos2⁡tdt
b
∫0π/2t4−2dt
c
∫0π/22t3−9dt
d
∫0π/22t2+3sin2⁡tdt
e
∫0π/2t−sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=3cos⁡t,y(t)=t2,z(t)=3sin⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(t2)j+ddt(3sin⁡t)k=−3sin⁡ti+2tj+3cos⁡tk.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Czdx+ydy−xdz=∫0π/2zdxdtdt+ydydtdt−xdzdtdt=∫0π/2(zdxdt+ydydt−xdzdt)dt=∫0π/23sin⁡t⋅(−3sin⁡t)+t2⋅(2t)−3cos⁡t⋅(3cos⁡t)dt=∫0π/22t3−9sin2⁡t−9cos2⁡tdt=∫0π/22t3−9dt

verification.explanation: Substitution gives zx'+yy'-xz'=-9sin²(t)+2t³-9cos²(t)=2t³-9. This confirms option c and agrees with the revealed worked solution. The incorrect submission selected a.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}z\,dx+y\,dy-x\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)={t}^{2},\,z(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}z\,dx+y\,dy-x\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}z\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(z\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{t}^{2}\cdot (2t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{t}^{3}-9{sin}^{2}⁡t-9{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{t}^{3}-9\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the line $r(t)=t\,i+2t\,j+3t\,k$ for $t\in [0,5]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=2t,\,z(t)=3t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j+3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$

$$

Question 10

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cy2dx+xdy+zdz, where C is a portion of the line r(t)=ti+2tj+3tk for t∈[0,5]?

a
∫054t2+11tdt
b
∫054t+5dt
c
∫05t2+10t+5dt
d
∫05t3+2dt
e
∫052t4−5tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t,y(t)=2t,z(t)=3t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(t)i+ddt(2t)j+ddt(3t)k=i+2j+3k.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cy2dx+xdy+zdz=∫05y2dxdtdt+xdydtdt+zdzdtdt=∫05(y2dxdt+xdydt+zdzdt)dt=∫054t2⋅(1)+t⋅(2)+3t⋅(3)dt=∫054t2+11tdt

content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the line $r(t)=t\,i+2t\,j+3t\,k$ for $t\in [0,5]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=2t,\,z(t)=3t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j+3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}({y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}4{t}^{2}\cdot (1)+t\cdot (2)+3t\cdot (3)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}4{t}^{2}+11t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since y dx+x dy=d(xy), the integral is the change in xy=8cos(t)sin(t)=4sin(2t). Thus its value is 4sin(π/2)−4sin(π/6)=4−2=2, giving option e.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{\pi }{4}].$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){|}_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Evaluate ∫C−1zdx+xdy+dz, where C is a portion of the helix parametrized by r(t)=cos⁡ti+tj+sin⁡tk for t∈[0,π].

a
2π
b
π
c
2+π4
d
π+2
e
2−π
Submit

decision.explanation: For 0<t<π, x=cos(t), y=t, z=sin(t), so −x'/z+xy'+z'=1+2cos(t). Although 1/z is undefined at the endpoints, the improper integral converges to [t+2sin(t)]₀^π=π. Thus option b is valid.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}-\frac{1}{z}\,dx+x\,dy+dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=t,\,z(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-\frac{1}{z}\,dx+x\,dy+dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{z}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\frac{1}{z}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\pi +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -0 \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: With x=t, y=t−1, and z=e^t, the integrand is (t−1)+t+e^(2t)=2t−1+e^(2t). Its integral from 0 to 1 is [t²−t+e^(2t)/2]₀¹=e²/2−1/2, giving option a.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(t-1)\,j+{e}^{t}\,k$ for $t\in [0,1].$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=t-1,\,z(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =i+j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-1)\cdot (1)+t\cdot (1)+{e}^{t}\cdot ({e}^{t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}+2t-1\,dt \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+{t}^{2}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}+1-1)-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t,y(t)=t−1,z(t)=et.

after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)={t}^{2}-1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\,dx+dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2t+{t}^{2}-1+1}{t}+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+t+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+3t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[2t+\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[2(2)+\frac{3}{2}(2)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[4+6] \\  & =10\end{aligned}
